title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself, say where you're from and what languages you speak, and ask other people the same.
intro:
In this unit you'll learn the personal pronouns — including Nepali's three levels of 'he/she' — and the two verbs 'to be'. Nepali uses **हो** to say *what* something is (identity) and **छ** to say *where* or *how* it is (location, state, existence). Getting these two right is one of the keys to sounding natural.

You'll also learn the essential question words and some survival phrases for when you don't understand.

vocab.note: For children, close friends, people younger than you. Rude about older adults.
Neutral, used for adults in news and writing; in speech a little distant.
For elders, teachers, guests — anyone you'd call तपाईं. Takes the same verb forms as तपाईं.
Dictionary form of both 'to be' verbs: हो (identity) and छ (location/state). Very irregular — see grammar.
Attached to the noun: अमेरिकाबाट 'from America', कहाँबाट 'from where'.
मैले बुझेँ 'I understood' / मैले बुझिनँ 'I didn't understand' (past forms take ले — unit 16).
मलाई नेपाली आउँछ 'I can speak Nepali' (lit. Nepali comes to me).
Same spelling as the possessive -को 'of', which is attached to a word.
Also used as a very polite 'you' in speeches.

phrases.en: I'm from Britain. (lit. I have come from Britain)

grammar.title: Pronouns and the identity verb हो
grammar.body:
**हो** links a subject to *what it is*: a name, a nationality, a job, a thing. It changes with the subject and its level of respect:

म **हुँ** *huṃ* · हामी **हौँ** *hauṃ*
तँ **होस्** *hos* · तिमी **हौ** *hau* · तपाईं **हुनुहुन्छ** *hunuhunchha*
ऊ / यो / त्यो **हो** *ho* · उनी **हुन्** *hun* · उहाँ **हुनुहुन्छ** · उनीहरू **हुन्** *hun*

Negative: म **होइनँ** *hoinaṃ*, हामी **होइनौँ**, तिमी **होइनौ**, ऊ **होइन**, उनीहरू **होइनन्**, तपाईं/उहाँ **हुनुहुन्न** *hunuhunna*.

Third person has three respect levels: **ऊ** (low), **उनी** (middle), **उहाँ** (high, same verb as तपाईं). In relaxed Kathmandu speech people often use plain **हो** with तपाईं in questions — तपाईं कहाँबाट हो? — and say म नेपाली होइन for होइनँ. You'll hear both; the full forms are always correct.

grammar.title: हो or छ? Two verbs 'to be'
grammar.body:
Nepali splits English 'to be' in two:

**हो** = identity/definition: *X is a Y*, *X is (the same as) Y*. ('This is tea.' 'I am a student.' 'It's me.')
**छ** = location, existence and state/description: *X is somewhere*, *there is an X*, *X is (in some condition)*. ('Tea is hot.' 'I'm in Kathmandu.' 'There's tea.')

छ conjugates: म **छु** · हामी **छौँ** · तँ **छस्** · तिमी **छौ** · ऊ **छ** · उनी/उनीहरू **छन्** · तपाईं/उहाँ **हुनुहुन्छ**.

Their negatives are different words too: हो → **होइन**, छ → **छैन** (म छैनँ, तिमी छैनौ, ऊ छैन, उनीहरू छैनन्, तपाईं हुनुहुन्न).

Quick test: if the English sentence ends in a *noun* ('…is a teacher'), use हो; if it ends in a *place* or a description of a temporary state ('…is at home', '…is tired', '…is good today'), use छ.

grammar.title: Question words
grammar.body:
Nepali question words begin with **k-**: के 'what', को 'who', कहाँ 'where', कुन 'which', कस्तो 'how/what kind', कसरी 'how (manner)', कति 'how much/many', किन 'why', कहिले 'when'.

They do **not** move to the front of the sentence. Put the question word where the answer would go — usually just before the verb: तपाईंको नाम **के** हो? = 'Your name **what** is?'

examples.en: Which country are you from? (lit. your country is which?)

dialogue.title: At the tea shop
dialogue.setting: Tom, an American student, sits down at a small tea shop in Patan. Ram, a local, starts chatting.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: मेरो नाम टम हो। तपाईंको नि?
lines.roman: mero nām Ṭam ho. tapāiṃko ni?

lines.speaker: Ram
lines.native: म राम हुँ। तपाईंलाई त नेपाली आउँछ!
lines.roman: ma Rām huṃ. tapāiṃlāi ta nepāli āuṃchha!
lines.en: I'm Ram. Hey, you speak Nepali!

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: अलिअलि मात्र। म यहाँ विद्यार्थी हुँ।
lines.roman: aliali mātra. ma yahāṃ bidyārthi huṃ.
lines.en: Only a little. I'm a student here.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.en: I live in Patan. And you?

lines.speaker: Ram
lines.native: म पनि यहीँ बस्छु। मेरो घर त्यहाँ छ।
lines.roman: ma pani yahiṃ baschhu. mero ghar tyahāṃ chha.
lines.en: I live right here too. My house is over there.

culture: Nepali is the **common language** of a very diverse country: for many Nepalis it is a second language after Newar (नेपाल भाषा), Maithili, Bhojpuri, Tamang, Tharu, Magar, Gurung, Rai or Limbu languages. So don't be surprised if two Nepalis switch to another language between themselves. In India, Nepali speakers in Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Sikkim often call themselves **Gorkha** and the language *Gorkhali*. Personal questions — age, marital status, salary, how much you paid for your phone — are normal friendly conversation, not rudeness; answer vaguely if you prefer.
